title: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
hook: a story of a sheet lifted from a body, and flowers underneath
carry: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
tomorrow: Ram or Allah: which name did Kabir call God?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed modern gurus and their cautions with two honest voices: devotion to the guru as to God, and follow only the good deeds. Today, a poet two communities kept.

Marigolds at a wedding, roses on a grave, jasmine pinned in someone's hair: flowers show up wherever people mark what matters. One story people tell ends in flowers. When the poet Kabir died, it goes, his followers gathered, Hindus and Muslims both. The Hindus wanted to cremate him. The Muslims wanted to bury him. The argument grew hot. Then someone lifted the sheet. No body. Only flowers. Each side took half, and went home.
screen: `MARIGOLDS, ROSES, JASMINE.` → `TWO COMMUNITIES, ONE BODY.` → `UNDER THE SHEET, FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: That's a legend, and it's told as one. The history underneath is just as striking. Kabir was a weaver in Benares, remembered as raised in a Muslim weaving family. He sang in the everyday speech of the street. His songs question empty ritual wherever he saw it, temple and mosque alike, and keep pointing to a God found within, close as the breath. And his verses traveled. Some are gathered in the Bijak, treasured by the Kabir Panth, the community that follows him. Others sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs. Hindus sing his couplets, and he's remembered among Muslims too. That's what this block means by a shared saint: someone more than one community remembers as its own. Taught as history, that rules a few things out. It doesn't erase real differences between Hindus and Muslims. It doesn't pretend the two always lived side by side in peace. And it doesn't claim Kabir for either side. It just looks at what happened: people across a line kept the same songs, and grieved over the same man. Look at the flowers again, too. Nobody in the story blends the two funerals into one. Each side carries its half home, and honors him its own way.
screen: `A LEGEND, TOLD AS ONE.` · `A WEAVER WHOSE SONGS TRAVELED.` · `REMEMBERED BY MORE THAN ONE.` · then, large: `HALF THE FLOWERS EACH.`

segments.voice: If there's a flower, a spice jar, a cup of tea or a piece of fruit near you, bring it close and breathe in its smell. Let it fill one breath, then another, slowly. A smell doesn't ask who you are before it reaches you; it reaches everyone in the room the same way. If there's nothing nearby, recall the scent of flowers at a gathering you've been to, and stay with it.
Hindu-Muslim shared saints: holy people like Kabir, remembered by more than one community as their own.
For the road: Hindu-Muslim shared saints, Kabir and the Sufis of the Deccan, taught as history, with half the flowers on each side. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you tell the flowers legend to your little cousin. she asks: so did they make one funeral for both of them?
options: no: each side took half, and honored him its own way.

fork.reveal: In the legend, the flowers are split, not mixed. A shared saint is honored by each community in its own way.
